Are there any plants of little value which could have been currently valuable had they been cultivated for centuries?
Would stone bramble be one of those plants?

Pretty much all "weeds" have medicinal or culinary use. Plantagos Major is an amazing antibiotic, Dandelion has almost every nutrient under the sun, wild lettuce is an anti-inflammatory. Aside from that "weeds" can be used to tell you what may or may not be wrong with your soil. If you have a lot of deep-rooted plants growing, you likely have compacted soil. Others can signal high salinity or a high amount of various toxins. I really hate the term weed because for most of human history all common plants had a purpose, a weed is a rosebush in a cornfield.
Obviously some weeds just fucking suck - like thistle and Bermuda grass. But most are really cool.
Bermuda Grass the yard of the south.

The short answer is yes. I think this is mostly through unidentified hybrids and breeding. Much of the current staple crops (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staple_food) are the result of inter-species hybridization. This can result in drastically different characteristics in the resulting species that can be beneficial to food production. In this sense, there may be many useless plants out there that when hybridized make delicious, nutritious valuable plants.

Crop cultivar development (breeding; I used to work at a breeding facility) results in much of the food you eat today. If you looked at bananas prior to cultivation and enhancement through selection they would be virtually inedible to most people. Little of the fleshy fruit and mostly seed with an odd flavor. The same could be said for most commercial crops for various reasons. In developing varieties through breeding we can essentially turn weeds into food. Back to your question, there are many "weeds" out there that have potential to be bred into viable food crops. This would be more obvious had they been cultivated and modified for centuries. Given new technology however there are many species that can be modified much more rapidly than it used to take so there may be new interesting foods in the future.

I dunno if this is going to answer the question directly, but I'd say sassafras albidum (American Sassafras) is probably more valuable than most people realize. Its wood is loaded with oil (about 6-9% by weight), so it makes it a really good choice for fires as the oil will keep the fire burning hotter and longer.

Aside from that though, sassafras leaves, roots and bark has been used medicinally for centuries, by the Native Americans and the British. One of the first exports of the Jamestown Colony, sassafras was employed by the Native Americans in the 16th century to ward off evil spirits and illness.

Since then, the oil, roots and bark are reported to have medicinal value as antiseptics, and analgesics. Sassafras's chemical component, safrole (found in leaves, roots and bark), is touted to have a wide variety of medicinal uses including treatment for scurvy, skin sores, kidney problems, toothaches, rheumatism, swelling, menstrual disorders and sexually transmitted diseases (syphilis and gonorrhea), bronchitis, hypertension, and dysentery.

It is also used as a fungicide, tooth cleaner, vasodilator to increase blood circulation, and to alleviate gastrointestinal problems. Two grams of the gum of the tree derived from sassafras pith can be used to treat inflammation, conjunctivitis, and erythema. The mild aromatic safrole oil from the bark can be made into a tea, or 5 to 10 drops can be placed on a sugar cube to treat kidney diseases, gastrointestinal problems, colds, rheumatism and skin inflammation. Five to ten drops, three times a day are recommended to treat gonorrhea or syphilis.

Also, the main component in the root bark, safrole, is the primary precursor for making MDMA and MDA, psychoactive drugs which are touted for their abilities to help treat/cure social anxiety, PTSD, and depression.

...

It really is a useful, beautiful, versatile tree. Aside from all of those medical uses and practical uses, it looks beautiful in the fall when its leaves turn into a vibrant sherbet candy orange, fading to red, and then purple. I've brewed old school root beer with it before. Great stuff, it is.
